Read the transcript of the audio guide
  1. Hedy Lamarr arrived in America in 1937 as a film star. source
  2. She was born Hedwig Eva Maria Kiesler in Vienna on 9 November 1914, the only child of a wealthy Jewish family. source
  3. She became an actress as a teenager. source
  4. Her first major role, in the Czechoslovak film Ecstasy, in 1933, made her famous and scandalous across Europe. source
  5. That same year she married Fritz Mandl, a wealthy munitions manufacturer and arms dealer. source
  6. In 1937 she left Mandl, and Austria. source
  7. She reached America by way of London, where she met the Hollywood studio boss Louis B. Mayer, who was looking for European talent. source
  8. Mayer gave her a new name, Hedy Lamarr, after his favorite silent-film star, Barbara La Marr. source
  9. A few months after she left, Nazi Germany annexed Austria. source
  10. Lamarr and her friend George Antheil, an avant-garde composer, were fierce opponents of the Nazis. source
  11. The trick was to keep changing the radio frequency. source
  12. A transmitter on a ship and a receiver in the torpedo would hop from frequency to frequency at the same moment, guided by matching paper rolls like those in a player piano. source
  13. They filed the patent on 10 June 1941. source
  14. Their patent explains: source
  15. In a conventional player piano record there may be 88 rows of perforations. source
  16. It was granted on 11 August 1942 as U.S. Patent 2,292,387, "Secret Communication System." source
  17. Hedy Lamarr became a United States citizen on 10 April 1953, sixteen years after she arrived, at a ceremony in federal court in Los Angeles. source
  18. In 2014 they were inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame. source
  19. What would you invent if you could work on any problem, with any partner?
Read the transcript of the short and the video
  1. Hedy Lamarr arrived in America in 1937 as a film star. source
  2. She left behind a husband who sold arms, a homeland about to be swallowed by Nazi Germany, and her father's fortune. source
  3. In the summer of 1941, a Hollywood film star filed a patent for a way to keep the enemy from jamming a torpedo. source
  4. She signed it with her legal name: Hedy Kiesler Markey. source
  5. The trick was to keep changing the radio frequency. source
  6. A transmitter on a ship and a receiver in the torpedo would hop from frequency to frequency at the same moment, guided by matching paper rolls like those in a player piano. source
  7. Hedy Lamarr became a United States citizen on 10 April 1953, sixteen years after she arrived, at a ceremony in federal court in Los Angeles. source
  8. Read the full story, with every source, on this page.
